about.title: About James Wolfe
about.body:
James writes on grace, patience, and the ordinary shape of the Christian life. He lives and works in a quiet Midwestern town, publishes on Substack twice monthly, reads often, and is always searching for sticks that might be swords.

## Mission

This site exists to help weary Christians find comfort and confidence in Christ — through writing that takes the ordinary, undramatic parts of faith seriously.

## Currently

Writing weekly, working on a first book, and slowly building out a public archive of quotations that have shaped his thinking.

articles.excerpt: Here’s the good news: Jesus brings us a radically better hope than anything you or I could possibly imagine. How? Well, I am now twenty nine; and once upon a time, Jesus was also twenty nine. And when God was my age, he had to wait.
articles.body:
Oh, I am *so* ready for my life to get going.

Yesterday, I turned twenty nine years old. I certainly don’t look or feel “almost thirty,” and part of me still anxiously looks over my shoulder anytime I’m out in public, half-expecting my old school principal to come up and say, *“I’m really sorry, we all made a terrible mistake letting you out there. You’re not really an adult at all. How on earth did you make it this far without anyone catching on?”*

But aside from debilitating levels of impostor syndrome and the ever-encroaching anxiety over my absconding sense of youth (my older friends are welcome to chortle at this one), there’s all kinds of waiting I have to navigate. For the last two years, I’ve felt like I’m just waiting for my life to get moving. And oh, how I hate the waiting. Even the healthiest theology will be challenged by the prospect of an unexpected wait.

Right now, I am…

* waiting for my career to kick off
* waiting to find a spouse and family
* waiting for guidance and direction
* waiting to finally feel like a real man
* waiting for my life to feel purposeful or meaningful in any way, like even a little bit.

And so I wait. What other choice do I have? I wait, and despair looms. I wait, and my waiting casts a shadow of claws and fangs. And as I wait, the waiting gnaws away at me, tearing little bite sized pieces of me away. I am feasted upon by my waiting.

You see, waiting often brings with it a little parasite. The medical term in the Latin is *invidia*, but most of us know it better by its common name: *envy*. Sometimes it crawls up into my mind, and at other times it clings to my heart; but most of the time it coils deep in my stomach, churning and devouring the good gifts of God, turning them into a poison brewed by impatience and frustration.

Envy is a filter — a negative one — that takes good things and transmutes them into waste. It takes ordinary waiting and turns it into a frustrated sense of lack. Envy always says, “I need more than what I have.” It only ever looks out, it is always starving, and though you could give it all the world, everything would never be enough.

Envy lies. *“This time of waiting you’re in? It means God has given up on you. Everyone else has the life that you want; you’re the only one who has to wait for your dreams. And you’re waiting for nothing, anyways. Those stupid dreams will always be out of reach. You’re stuck — hopelessly stuck — and you’re never, ever getting out.”*

Sound familiar?

But here’s the good news: **Jesus brings us a radically better hope than anything you or I could possibly imagine.** How? Well, I am now twenty nine; and once upon a time, Jesus was also twenty nine.

And when God was my age, he had to wait.

* When Jesus was 29, the radiance of the glory of God worked in a rural carpentry shop doing menial tasks, waiting for his ministry to begin.
* When Jesus was 29, he who would conquer the tyranny of death through the power of his own blood would wait and watch his earthly father die.
* When Jesus was 29, he who would one day sit forever at the right hand of the throne of the Father, enthroned in glory — at whose feet would angels fall and sing in unceasing chorus, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was, and is, and is to come,” and, “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created” — that guy didn’t do a single thing history thought worth recording.
* In fact, at 29 Jesus didn’t seem to be doing much at all.
* He was just… waiting.

He waited quietly, spending decades in total obscurity and seeming irrelevance, waiting for the Father’s time to be made right. And that waiting was, to an almighty, sovereign God, apparently very, very good.

:::scripture Lamentations 3:25-26
“The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord.”
:::

Our God is Lord of all who are waiting. And he is so, so good.

What a comfort to know that Jesus waited too! What more proof do we need that our waiting isn’t a waste? If our Savior chose not to rush through his periods of drought and doldrums, but waited and submitted himself to the Father’s will, then why should we be any different? Why should we let envy and impatience steal our joy in this moment, now — in waiting?

Biblical history is primarily a description of people who wait. Israel waited while in the bondage of slavery, displaced in the desert, lost in exile, and through 400 years of painful silence. Every prophet, patriarch, priest and king was someone who waited. Every account in scripture that has inspired you has almost certainly involved a painful period of protracted waiting. So, too, is the Christian’s life marked by our waiting, as we must all of us ultimately wait for Christ to return. “To be Christian,” as Mark Vroegop says, “is to wait.”

:::scripture Psalm 130:5-6
“I wait for the Lord, my soul waits, and in his word I hope; my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning.”
:::

So no, your waiting is not a waste. It is good that you are waiting right now. It is good that I am waiting right now. The Lord is good to you and to me and to everyone who waits in hope on the word of his promise. Yes, Christian, he is unbelievably good to you. Even in your waiting.

So now I am twenty nine, and I am still waiting to see what will come of my life. But rather than waiting anxiously, wracked with envy and frustration, I can wait joyfully, filled with a durable, secure hope that God will not fail to complete the good work he has begun in me. And I can run this race with endurance, setting aside every weight and sin that clings so closely, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of my faith — the same Jesus who was twenty nine once, and also had to wait for his life to get started.

You were able to be saved because Jesus waited. He waited in perfect obedience, not rushing ahead into his own desire, but resting in the knowledge that the Father’s time is always best. And that act of waiting was redeemed into the greatest glory that history has ever known.

What do you think God can do with your waiting?

articles.title: When Jesus Turned 29

articles.excerpt: I’m pretty helpless before that condemning voice. So in the end, I have no choice but to accept that I am completely unable to evaluate my own appearance; I am simply not an objective judge of my own self. I need a better standard.
articles.body:
Most days, I don’t recognize my own reflection.

There’s no hidden symbolism in that sentence — I genuinely just have trouble recognizing who I see in the mirror each morning. It’s weird. After about 6-12 months of hard exercise, I’ve put on about twenty five pounds of muscle. It took a lot of discipline, but it feels good. As a result, my body has gone from “worryingly skinny” to “slightly less worryingly skinny.” Truly, a Grecian statue; I have achieved the pinnacle of the masculine form.

But in all seriousness, while that kind of growth *is* rewarding progress, it doesn’t reflect any kind of radical transformation: I’ve filled out a little bit in my elbows and chest, put on a little volume in my arms, and that’s about it. Don’t get me wrong, I’m proud of the progress. Small gains become the sum of their parts, and the result has been pretty meaningful to a naturally skinny guy like me. But we’re talking about incremental changes, not sudden transformation. So while some of my clothes may fit a little more snugly, and while I may get a few extra glances around town, at the end of the day I’m still just me: a guy who is visually identifiable as a *writer* and not ever as a *football* player*.*

But as small as the changes are, and as humble as the growth has been, something inside me rebels; I still feel like this body doesn’t belong to me. I feel like I stole someone’s identity. I’m confronted almost every day with a self-image my mind can’t easily accept. In my mind, I am still unhealthily thin. Even this astonishingly small change has been (I’m more than a little self-conscious to admit) startling and disrupting to my self-perception.

It’s a kind of body dysmorphia — a minor, harmless one in my case, although for others it can present far more seriously. This dysmorphia supplants the evidence of my eyes, displacing the body that I actually have with an old body that I remember. And it lies. *Yes*, I have grown stronger. *Yes,* I look stronger and healthier. *No*, I am not the sad result of a drunken night of passion between a dejected skeleton and a squeaky rubber chicken — although as origin stories go, that one totally rocks.

And despite this dazzling, near-superhuman feat of athletic achievement that I’ve so dazzlingly and athletically achieved, in my mind my body still invites comparison to that sad little tree from the Charlie Brown Christmas special. Yes, I still picture myself as some kind of long-lost cousin to one of those gangly, inflatable dancing guys you see in front of the *coolest* used car dealerships.

God sure knows how to keep me humble.

All the work I’ve been doing? Boy, it’s *working*. But I still feel tiny, thin, and weak. I feel like I’m always cosplaying as someone who doesn’t look totally ridiculous at every moment of every day. And now I have a condemning voice on loop that tells me that I will always be exactly how I perceive, and that nothing will ever, *ever* change that. No matter how much I work out, I *know* that I’ll always be hideously thin. It’s totally crazy. And in the end, I’m pretty helpless before that voice. So in the end, I have no choice but to accept that I am completely unable to evaluate my own appearance; I am simply not an objective judge of my own self. I need a better standard.

And I suspect that many Christians aside from me face this exact same struggle when it comes to our spiritual lives.

Because in the same way that dysmorphia prevents me from perceiving my own body correctly, **spiritual dysmorphia prevents all of us from seeing our own lives according to the objective truths of who we are in Christ.**

:::scripture 1 John 3:19-20
“By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.”
:::

For many of us, that condemning voice has an awful lot to say: about our lives, our identities, and the security of our salvation. It forces us to see ourselves perpetually in terms of who we once were, or who we think we ought to be, instead of on the objective basis of what the gospel insists is true of us. We don’t accept the changes that have been made, whether incremental or immediate, as a result of the free gift of transformation and renewal that the gospel of Jesus brings to us *right now*.

In the same way that dysmorphia forces me to obsess over my perceived physical deficiencies, spiritual dysmorphia compels us to see ourselves only in terms of lack. It feeds us an endless buffet of lies, and we are only too happy to pay the bill.

We stare at our reflections and we hear:

* Your heart is truly hideous.
* All your desires turn towards sin.
* Your whole life is unbelievably selfish.
* Everything about you screams “hopeless.”
* No part of you could never please God.

**But the reflection lies.**

John explains this in his first letter. When you are in Christ, the voice of truth will reassure you, not condemn you. When it comes to your truest identity, there is no condemnation that can share any space with the most crucial facts about you. However you choose to describe yourself in Christ, you can only possibly be reassured by what you find. So whenever your heart condemns you with voices like those above, you can tell it that God is greater than your heart, and that he knows *everything*.

You can tell yourself what God knows:

* He knows your broken heart.
* He knows your sinful desires.
* He knows your dodgy motives.
* He knows your fearful future.
* He knows every single part of you.

And at the end of all that knowing, he still eagerly calls you his beloved child. His heart swells in love for you; his affections are unyielding and his love is energetic. He rejoices in your victories and grieves over your sorrows. Yes, you may know that you are a hopeless failure that God could never love, fix, use, or redeem; and yes, you may know that you are ugly, twisted, and wretched beyond all hope of love. But God knows better. Whatever condemnation you may think you know to be true, God has something better to say. **He is greater than your heart.**

God knew exactly who you were when he chose you. He knew your future, your every mistake, and every aspect of you that most makes you cringe. He knew all that, and he chose you with joy. You are his beloved child, never to be cast out, and raised to the highest place with Christ. So that reflection you despise? God sees something vastly different. What he sees in you, he loves — he isn’t ever embarrassed to be associated with you.

Oh yes, that reflection lies.

And we can’t do this alone. God has given us a gift to help us live in the light of truth more readily: he has given us a community of believers to walk with us in faith, hope, and love through all things. So let those around you bring encouragement:

:::scripture Hebrews 12:1-2
“Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith.”
:::

When I can’t see the growth that God has made in my life — the incremental transformation of a thousand days of daily acts of obedience — I have people around me who can point me to the truth. They tell me what I fundamentally cannot see when my eyes are blinded by dysmorphic reflections. That God **has** changed me. That by his grace, I **can** continue to grow and learn. I can throw off the weight and sin that clings so closely, keep running this race, and look to Christ, who loves me and chose me. I can’t see it; I can hardly believe it. But good friends can. And they tell me when I can’t tell myself.

So if spiritual dysmorphia is telling you that you haven’t ever changed or grown, it’s probably lying. But don’t take my word for it — bring your fears to other believers. Tell them how you feel, and see what they have to say. I would be shocked if any mature Christian who you’ve been in close community with for longer than 3-4 months could not point to one or many ways in which you have demonstrated some kind of growth in the ways of Christ, in the fruits of the spirit. It might be subtle, or not what you were hoping for, but God has promised to complete the good work he began in you. You’re just too close to see what he’s done.

You are not a good mirror. Let others hold the mirror up for you.

When you submit your life to Christ as Lord, you have to submit your insecurities as well. You are not given the option: you can no longer be meaningfully defined in any capacity by anything except that which you can find in the fountain of blood that flows from Christ. He is your one true mirror, the one place your reflection will not cast dimly, and the only source by which you will discover the answers to every question that haunts you. So come behold your Savior.

Scripture tells us that as we behold this Christ, we will be transformed into that same image, day by day — incrementally, by this “long obedience in the same direction.” So no, perhaps you don’t recognize your reflection in the mirror. But perhaps that isn’t true because of how awful you are. Perhaps that’s true because the reflection you see looks a little more like Christ than it did yesterday.

And when you are in Christ, that reflection never lies.

articles.title: The Mirror Lies

articles.excerpt: God does not see hindrances. Insofar as it’s possible, I don’t believe he knows the word. He laughs at your inability, your weakness, your smallness – not because he agrees with any of that, but because he knows how little those words mean. What you believe are impossible hindrances in your life, what you perceive as disqualifying limitations, what you know for a fact are paralyzing incapabilities – God smiles at those things, because he sees abundant opportunities.
articles.body:
I’ve read your mind: I know exactly what you want. What, you don’t believe me? I’ll tell you.

You secretly want to be perceived as foolish, small, and weak. Oh, you can try to hide it all you want, but I know how much you want to be mocked, derided, brought low, and despised. Yes, you scoff at those who want to be well-liked, powerful, influential, and wise. The fools! 

“A promotion?” you may ask derisively. “No, I’d much rather stamp buttons at the button stamping factory until I die uninsured and alone from button related injuries.” 

You may have thought you were special, but you’re no different from the rest of us: your deepest aspiration in life is to be as unimportant and insignificant as possible, to never change a single thing, and to one day die completely forgotten, if indeed anybody ever knew you at all.

How am I doing so far? I can only assume I’m *totally nailing it*, right?

Despite my well-earned confidence, this is, of course, completely ridiculous. None of us, even the most earnestly humble, could actually say any of that stuff and mean it. And I’m not sure any of us should. We don’t want to be smaller, and we don’t aspire to be seen as lesser, much less weak or foolish. The reality is that all of us want exactly the opposite. We would all like to be stronger, wiser, greater, better liked, more influential, more desirable, and more visible. We want to be bigger. We’d like to be more capable.

And we can aspire to those things for genuinely good ends. We may want to be stronger and wiser so that we can have a greater impact as we serve God and our communities. We can aspire to greatness, capability, and influence because doing so gives us more reach as we try to spread the gospel and build up our communities in love. Knowing that we are living witnesses to the testimony of the gospel of Christ, *of course* we would want to be well liked, winsome, and visible.

The “twist” of this post is not to tell you that any of those things are bad. They are all good! I sure hope so, anyways. For crying out loud, I’m building a writing platform, and I very much want it to succeed – and while I can be an astonishing hypocrite on many occasions, I don’t think this is one of them. There are plenty of good reasons to desire and aspire for the more obviously positive qualities mentioned rather than those that seem far more like hindrances.

But what fascinates me is how scripture doesn’t actually treat the former list as hindrances at all. In fact, when you read the story of God’s people, you begin to see how he uses nobody except for foolish, small, weak people. And when you read Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, you can especially see a totally different list begin to emerge.

Because what we see as weaknesses to overcome, God sees as *qualifications*.

:::scripture 1st Corinthians 1:26-27
“For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong.”
:::

I’ve spent much of the last two weeks frustrated by feelings of my own incapability. It doesn’t really matter what it is – even the simplest things the last few weeks have just felt overwhelming and too big for me to handle. I’m constantly bombarded with choices, and it feels like I only ever screw those choices up. Looking back, I have a trail of regrets to make Hansel and Gretel proud. It’s just too much. I am weak. I am small. I am foolish. It feels painfully obvious. Much like the church in Corinth, I’m just not the guy I wish I was. There are so many ways I let myself down every single day, and the days don’t stop coming.

And amidst all those choices, it’s easy for me to feel like I’m not just letting myself down, but God. Because when I’m not pursuing my highest calling as a writer, or failing to adequately optimize my financial future, or because another Saturday went by where I basically didn’t get off the couch, I just know that God isn’t able to use me. Because I didn’t live up to *my* standards, God is disappointed in me. And because I failed to be disciplined, God has no choice but to move on to the next guy. And that dude is probably way better looking too. With abs.

Yes, I’m aware of how ridiculous my brain is when I let it into the sunlight. But don’t think too badly of me – you’d be amazed how poorly your practical theology holds up to scrutiny. The point is, we all hold incredibly foolish beliefs, and these aren’t new thoughts. I don’t own them. Why do you think Paul felt the need to remind the church in Corinth not to feel discouraged by weaknesses that they felt were impossible hindrances? *Because they felt discouraged by weaknesses that they thought were impossible hindrances.*

And we’re no different.

God does not see hindrances. Insofar as it’s possible, I don’t believe he knows the word. He laughs at your inability, your weakness, your smallness – not because he agrees with any of that, but because he knows how little those words mean. What you believe are impossible hindrances in your life, what you perceive as disqualifying limitations, what you *know for a fact* are paralyzing incapabilities – God smiles at those things, because he sees abundant opportunities.

He’s like a kid in a sandbox, with nothing to hold him back from making the *coolest* thing out of nothing but sand and glitter and dirt that got in by mistake.

He chooses weak people; and he doesn’t choose them by mistake.

:::scripture 1st Corinthians 1:28-31
“God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God. And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
:::

If you are in Christ, you can boast in the Lord. Your weaknesses are nothing; those hindrances are empty. He chooses the things that you despise in yourself to do some of his greatest work. That means the very things that most humiliate you are the parts he is the most excited for. The most shameful parts of you that cause you to shrink away are the very things that God will use, so that you can boast, “My God is so great.”

So there is no brokenness that can separate you from his love.

There is no weakness that can remove you from his plan.

There is no foolishness that can make him despise you.

There is no shame that can cause him to see you as insignificant.

There is nothing that can cause God’s plan for you to be defeated. And his plan for you is so, so good, so much better than you could ever believe.

It may not be the case that you *want* to be weak, or foolish, or small. It isn’t wrong to try to better yourself. But there’s no reason to be scared of those things either. When it turns out that you really are weak, or you actually have been foolish, or you truly are quite small and powerless, that’s no reason to be discouraged. It’s only one part of a story, and it only gets better from here.

So no, there’s nothing inherently virtuous or admirable about being great. Sure, it’s fine, but if you’re looking for something to boast in, you won’t find it there. But being small? Now there’s something to be excited about.

Christian, trust God and be small.
articles.author: James Wolfe
articles.title: Christian, Be Small

articles.excerpt: Just as that gift from the donor would give you impenetrable material security, the gift of God in salvation gives you an impenetrable spiritual security. And while the material will pass away, the spiritual is eternal. The steadfast love of God means that you can’t ruin your life more than he can save it. It means that you can’t waste your life so much that he can’t redeem it. It means you can never yourself dig so deep that he’ll give up on you. Nothing can separate.
articles.body:
You wake up tomorrow and discover that an anonymous donor has given you a free gift of ten million dollars. What’s more, he’s set up investment accounts in your name so that even if you squander his gift, you can live comfortably and securely for the rest of your life without working. You find that your bills are all paid from this account, your mortgage is paid off, and any student loans are wiped clean. You also find that a mechanic came overnight and has completely tuned up your car so that it will run smoothly for another 150,000 miles.

More than that, you get a letter from this donor saying that when you retire, he has a private villa prepared for you to live in, with you, your family, and any friends who want to join you. You receive invitations to come and celebrate every holiday with his own family, and you aren’t expected to provide anything but yourself; and when you do bring something, everyone makes it out to be the best part of the meal, even if it was just a small store-bought dish. All his family genuinely loves you, and they delight to include you in everything.

Through this donor, the best lawyer in the world is hired on permanent retainer in your name, and he advocates for you in any kind of legal dispute such that you know you’ll never have to fear any accusation ever again. A little later on, you learn that this donor is also running a comprehensive PR campaign for you as well, telling everyone in his contacts list how excited he is to know you. And after learning all this, you receive a handwritten letter from this donor that reads, *“If you need anything else, just ask, and I’ll move heaven and earth to take care of you.”*

What do you do? How long does it take for you to realize that this offer is genuine? When does it “click,” and you realize that you have every one of your deepest desires, that every need is lavishly met, and that you never have to earn anything ever again?

**And why, if this is true for us, do we live like it isn’t?**

:::scripture Romans 8:31-32
“What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?”
:::

The last couple of months I’ve been paralyzed by the fear that I’m wasting my life. An irrational thought, maybe, but none the less formidable. Despite the frequent reassurances from godly counsel that I am, in fact, doing everything that could be expected of me at this age, I can’t shake the feeling that they’re all missing what is abundantly clear to me:

\- That I’m actually a total fraud, squandering away my best years;

\- That God is frequently disappointed in how I apportion my time;

\- And that the only hope I have to please God is to work so much harder than I already am.

It’s a suffocating and disquieting way to live, an extraordinarily heavy weight to carry.

And it’s entirely unnecessary.

Because if that story a few paragraphs up was true for me, I can tell you that I wouldn’t feel pressured to work another day in my life. Oh, can you imagine being totally free of all worries, choosing each day’s activities without worry or constraint, knowing that every need is richly and abundantly met? How unbelievable that would be if it were true!

**And yet it is true.** That inheritance is yours.

God has richly poured out every blessing on you and me, and evaporated the power of all our deepest fears. Nothing can separate; nothing can destroy. You have such a donor, except he isn’t anonymous. He has provided you with riches, a future, a home, a family, love, safety, belonging, and rest. Any problem you can anticipate has already been answered in your favor. You won’t find the riches of Christ in your bank account or driveway, but they’ll outlast every market, country, and kingdom on earth. **You don’t need to earn anything else ever again.** You already have it all.

You’ve won.

What you’ve won is like the best lottery in the world – and you didn’t even know you had entered. You thought you came to Jesus just because you were so bad; you probably never imagined that he could treat you so good. And because of what he’s done for you, you’re *untouchable*. There is no problem that his riches and advocacy can’t shatter like clay. You are forever safe, forever secure. You have the ultimate advocate. You have an infinite inheritance. **Your future is invincibly secure.**

When you are in Christ, no worry or hurt you suffer can ever outweigh the magnitude of his gift – your salvation. In Christ, you’re a spiritual millionaire. More than that, even; for the best part of the gift is Christ himself, and his value is beyond all measuring.

:::scripture Romans 8:38-39
“For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
:::

I don’t know what you would do the day after you find ten million dollars in your bank account, but I’m pretty sure you wouldn’t go back to your job at the shoelace factory. And when it comes to your biggest problem, there’s nothing left to do – it’s already done! You’ve won the lottery. It’s right there, sitting in your account, ready to use. No matter your problems, you have enough buoyancy to stay afloat through any trouble.

Just as that gift from the donor would give you impenetrable material security, **the gift of God in salvation gives you an impenetrable spiritual security.** And while the material will pass away, the spiritual is eternal. The steadfast love of God means that you can’t ruin your life more than he can save it. It means that you can’t waste your life so much that he can’t redeem it. It means you can never yourself dig so deep that he’ll give up on you. Nothing can separate.

And nobody else can separate you either. No, nothing can separate you from the love of God in Christ. God is for you! So who or what on earth could be against you? You’re safe.

We may fear the offer of that donor. We fear it because we didn’t earn it, we don’t deserve it, and we can’t control it. **But this gift being beyond our earning means it’s beyond our ruining as well.** It’s yours – forever! Christ signed the contract in his own blood so that nothing could ever break or undermine it. And because you are ridiculously, stupidly, abundantly rich in Christ... you can rest.

Yes, rest. Rest from your need for validation, from your striving towards nothing, from that aching desire that’s burning a hole in your heart. Rest from every injustice you face, every hurt you feel, every trial you endure. Come to Jesus, accept his gift, and find your rest in him. He is gentle and lowly in spirit, and he dwells with the weak and downtrodden. He is absurdly rich, and loves nothing more than giving all his wealth away.

So yes, I am weary from all my striving.

*But I rejoice in the finished, invincibly secure work of Christ.*

And I am anxious of my spiritual poverty.

*But I rejoice in the incomprehensibly vast riches of Christ.*

I lament the man that I have failed to be.

*But I rejoice in the relentless, unassailable love of Christ that covers all of my failure.*

For nothing can separate you, nothing can condemn you, and nothing can impoverish you. You can’t enrich yourself any more – you already have it all! You can’t break it, lose it, or spend too much of it. You don’t need to be cautious, or tepid, or restrained with this gift. Draw from his riches as much as you need, take unrestrainedly from his mercy and grace, dive into his oceans of love without caution or reserve. You’re free to enjoy the gift for the rest of your life, or to work unpressured for pleasure, or to give the gift to others around you. The choice is yours.

The only choice that doesn’t make sense is to keep working and striving like you have anything left to earn.

Because there isn’t anything left to earn.

*It’s already done.*
articles.author: James Wolfe
articles.title: It's Already Done

articles.excerpt: The cry of all these hearts is a universal one. “Why does my life have to be this way?” Scripture rarely answers every “why” that we ask. Instead, it shows us what God is doing and where he is leading us. Yet we all have felt that question forced out of us, whether through a brief flash of pain, or while enduring long seasons of relentless afflictions, the kind that feel dominating, life-defining, and eternal.
articles.body:
Jeremiah was a prophet, one of the highest callings among God’s covenant people. He was tasked with delivering the words of the Lord to his people, and he did. He was obedient the first time, he spoke God’s message, and delivered some of the greatest and most monumental prophecies in all of scripture.

Shortly after, he cursed the day he was born, saying that it would have been better if he had died in his mother’s womb.

Elijah, another prophet, was perhaps one of the greatest workers of miracles in biblical history. God used him to bring judgement down on wicked kings, to shatter idols, and to deliver the kind of radical change and societal reform that most of us can only dream of. He witnessed God’s might and majesty in ways that probably none of us ever will in this life.

After his greatest triumph, he ran away in fear and shame, and begged God to let him die.

Hannah served God with all her heart, and was loved lavishly by her husband. She lived in prosperous and peaceful times. She was respected in her community, had the favor of God, and the love of a good man, yet her one grief overshadowed all her blessings.

She wept and prayed with such bitterness and insensible grief that Eli the priest thought she was drunk.

The cry of all these hearts is a universal one. *“Why does my life have to be this way?”* Scripture rarely answers every “why” that we ask. Instead, it shows us what God is doing and where he is leading us. Yet we all have felt that question forced out of us, whether through a brief flash of pain, or while enduring long seasons of relentless afflictions, the kind that feel dominating, life-defining, and eternal.

But no matter our experience, we know and can affirm that others have felt the same – these voices in scripture and more. And as we wrestle with the same questions and fears that they lifted up, we may well ask why we have these accounts written down, preserved as God’s eternal word for us. There are many reasons, but I want to point us to three.

1. They are written for our comfort.
2. They are written to show God’s glory.
3. They are written to record how we might be transformed by the power of the gospel.

:::scripture 2nd Corinthians 4:16-18
“So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.”
:::

#### 1. Our comfort.

Do you ever feel alone in your hard feelings? Scripture is here to tell you that you are never alone – whether in despair, depression, anxiety, neediness, or bitter longing. You are a part of God’s story, just as those who came before you, and you are not alone. Others have felt these things before you; your feelings and cries for help are not shameful.

But better than just company, you get a destination. You get to see where each of their stories took them in the end. Jeremiah is vindicated; Elijah ascended; Hannah had the child of her prayers. While the weight of your present story may suffocate you now, where could it take you next? You only have to look at what God has done for others, and know that he will be just as faithful to you as he was to them. And in the end, you know that Christ has walked with you then, and now, and always, and he is no stranger to affliction.

Whether in this life or in heaven, your story is building towards a magnificent crescendo – an eternal weight of glory that will make all these light momentary afflictions seem like nothing at all.

#### 2. God’s glory.

Do you long for meaning in your story? Do you ever feel like everything you do is pointlessly hard? Scripture demonstrates that every act of obedience, while they may not make sense right now, are nothing less than a successive layering of bricks in the radiant temple of God’s glorious dwelling. What feels meaningless means everything.

You contribute to God’s glory – not adding to it, but participating in it. Your life, for all that it might feel petty and mean, reverberates in an unseen world beyond all your reckoning. Everything matters; nothing goes unseen. What you perceive as worthless, God counts as glorious. Your treasure may be carried in jars of clay, but the surpassing power of your story belongs to God, not you. Your weakness is his strength.

So you may not understand the chaos of your life now – just like the reverse side of a cross-stitch embroidery reveals nothing but tangled skeins of thread – but one day it will flip, and you will see all your life with eyes that burn with the eternal, and all that seemed like chaos will be made known for what it always was: the glory of God, shining through your life, radiant and unfettered.

#### 3. Transformation.

Do you feel crushed beneath an impossible weight? Have you seen your hopes wither and fade? Scripture promises two things: You will not lose heart. You will be transformed.

You are two selves. There is your outer self, which is being crushed and broken, which is wounded and frail, which feels the weight of the world and breathes the poisons of evil every day. And there is your inner self, which is being renewed day by day, transformed from glory to glory as you behold the glory of God. Your old self must be crucified daily. Yes, crucifixion is ugly, brutal, horrific, and painful. It will hurt. You will have to give some things up. But you are not better than Christ; nor are you better than his cross. Take it up with him and follow him into death. His death is the kind that brings life.

And because of this paradoxical death-life, you can bear the weights and griefs of this world, you can suffer the slings and arrows of hurt, and you can keep from losing heart. Because every tear now will be laughter later, every wound now will be a future treasure. There is nothing in this present age, not one moment of suffering, that you will not see transformed through Christ into comfort and glory and eternal life – if only you will put your trust in Him, and surrender your life to his Lordship.

- - -

There are still tears. Pain is still real. Sorrow still hurts just as much. Jeremiah still wept; Elijah still broke down; Hannah still pleaded. None of them saw their stories in full. They all saw with veiled faces, and despaired.

But we have Christ. And in him, the veil is removed. Christian, you know where your story ends! Your story ends in renewal, in transformation, in laughter, in joy, in a bright glory that will outshine the sun, in a warm embrace that will never let go. Your story ends before the throne of God, and it ends in worship, and it is an ending that will never end, but will continue for all of eternity.

So you may still ask that question, “Why does my life have to be this way?” But you have the answer.

Your life in all its afflictions is preparing you for an eternal weight of glory. Your real life is unseen, invisible; yet one day it will spring into reality, more real than anything you’ve ever seen, heard, touched, tasted, or felt. And on that day, your broken, battered self will be revealed to be something different, something new, something you never thought it could be.

You will be transformed.

You will be renewed.

You will be glorious.

And you will have Christ.

So don’t lose heart. This gentle road of afflictions is just how you get there.
articles.author: James Wolfe
articles.title: Why does my life have to be this way?

articles.excerpt: When I step out that door, even with an earbud in, I can’t hear what I’m listening to. All of the calm, quiet life I need in my ear gets drowned out by the oppressive, industrial clamor of the factory. So I make God loud.
articles.body:
The office connects to the factory by a brief and narrow hallway, concluding at a thin plywood door that has seen better days. It’s a fragile but effective barrier between the two worlds: one administrative, the other industrial.

When you open that door, you will experience several things.

First, the heat. A wave of stifling, unconditioned air will rush over you in a moment. You’ll breathe it in, feel the moisture condense on your skin and in your lungs. Some days, that heat will make your eyes water.

Next the sight. Cleanliness will become a myth; colors will thin to a narrow definition of rusty browns, industrial greys, and engulfing blacks. You’ll feel a thin film of oil on any exposed surface you make the mistake of touching.

Then, sensation. The grit of ten thousand metal shavings will crunch beneath your feet; you’ll breathe in grimy smoke and metallic dust, dodge the lightning-flash of sparks as you pass the grinders, swelter in the convection heat of acetylene torches as you walk through brazing.

Finally comes the sound. Silence is a memory on the factory floor, as all the industrial cacophony surrounds you at once. Grinding wheels, shifting gears, screeching metals, coolant spray, and the inescapable shout of a hundred competing fans.

And above it all, the radio.

Deafening as the factory is, the radio always manages to clamor over it. It is constant, predictable, and unpleasant. Yes, the heat may be dizzying, and the view grim and apocalyptic, but if you’re lucky, the music might be tolerable every once in a while.

But you work at a factory. Most days are not very lucky.

I usually have at least one earbud in throughout the work day. I mostly listen to a mixture of worship music, Tim Keller sermons, and Gavin Ortlund podcasts. It helps keep me sane. I like to think that I keep God in one ear, whispering to me all day through “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” alongside the “teaching and admonishing” of Colossians 3:16. It makes the hard days bearable.

But when I step out that door, crossing the threshold from the office into the shop, the noise and presence of the factory floor overwhelms me. It’s loud. Some would say blaring. When I step out that door, even with an earbud in, I can’t hear what I’m listening to. All of the calm, quiet life I need in my ear gets drowned out by the oppressive, industrial clamor of the factory.

So I make God loud.

Before I open the factory door, I turn my earbuds up exactly three clicks. It doesn’t matter then what’s on the radio, or whether one of the grinding wheels has chosen that particular moment to screech like a territorial rooster, or whether some of the guys are cussing at each other across the floor – no matter how loud it gets, the quiet voice in my ear is louder still. Three clicks, and I drown out all the clamor around me.

I think the same principle can be true of our lives. Just as crossing the factory threshold invites an overwhelming clamor of sensations, stepping out into the world comes at an equivalent cost. As the clamor of busyness, and the stifling weariness of heartache, and the long oppression of suffering overwhelm us, it can be easy to let those loud voices be the ones that define our day to day. Because they are loud, they seem near; because they seem near, we think of them first.

But as loud as those voices are, let God be louder still.

Be jealous of your time with God. Cherish your devotional times. Linger in prayer and in scripture, and let those words return to you throughout each day. Consider your spiritual walk as being like a desert nomad hopping from one oasis to the next, drinking in all the life she can get to sustain her from one cool and shaded spring to the next. Turn the volume up.

Ruminate on scripture, not your troubles, that you might be “complete, equipped for every good work.” Discover a few trusted psalms to return to, words of comfort to “calm and quiet” your soul. Remember at all times that the Lord is “good to those who wait on him.” Return in your heart to the one who is “gentle and lowly in spirit,” who will give you rest. Turn the volume up.

Don’t try to do what you can’t control. This world is dark, and full of suffering. The people around you will be selfish, rude, thoughtless, vile, and cruel. You will never be fully sufficient to meet all the troubles of your world without being shaken and unmoored. You can never turn the world’s volume down. But you are not helpless. 

Turn the volume up.

On Monday I will go back to the factory. I will walk down that hallway, and I will stop outside that door. When I open it, I will feel the heat, see the oil-stained floors, smell the smoke and dust and old rusty metal, and feel crunching grit beneath my sneakers. But I will not hear the industrial clamor and metallic screeching and the overbearing radio.

Because I will turn my earbuds three clicks louder.

And I will drown out the clamor of the world with the gentle voice of truth.

I will make God loud.
articles.author: James Wolfe
articles.title: Make God Loud

authors.name: James Wolfe
authors.bio: James writes on grace, patience, and the ordinary shape of the Christian life. He lives and works in a quiet Midwestern town, publishes on Substack twice monthly, reads often, and is always searching for sticks that might be swords.
